content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting pieces of news about next year's iPhone; the device, seen as the iPhone's twentieth-anniversary commemorative model, is also said to be the concrete realisation of Apple's long-standing vision of "a single sheet of glass."

As for what we can realistically expect, conflicting reports have been circulating, but yesterday's divergence was arguably the most dramatic to date…

Where things currently stand

Apple's former design chief Jony Ive has frequently spoken of his long-term vision of eventually turning the iPhone into "a single sheet of glass"; even though Ive has left the company, there remains a widespread belief that Apple is moving in this direction.

Although Apple generally does not celebrate anniversaries in a big way, the consensus is that they want to get as close as possible to realising this vision before the iPhone's twentieth anniversary. This could include embedding Face ID under the display and hiding the front-facing camera beneath the screen.

However, we have already seen conflicting reports on these expectations. The original view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports suggest this design will appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In terms of naming convention, that would make it the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple could also choose to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday's situation became even more muddled when an analyst claimed that Apple had abandoned the idea of launching an all-glass iPhone next year.

But Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately pushed back against this claim.

What is more likely the reality

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone does not have a single end point. What they plan to launch next year is just one step—or several steps—towards that sci-fi vision of "a single sheet of glass."

The question is not whether this goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will go in this direction. But whether it is one step or several, this is certainly not the final step in the evolution of iPhone design.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has actually pulled back somewhat from what were previously expected to be next year's targets.

The analyst at Jefferies likely received the same information, but a beat slower, and mistakenly assumed that the entire plan had been shelved.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap forward—comparable to the breakthrough of the iPhone X—but there will be further developments in the years to come. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will feature a breakthrough large enough to warrant some form of special branding, such as being labelled as the twentieth-anniversary iPhone (which I think is unlikely), being bestowed a special name, or being skipped a generation to be called the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
